note: Produces tamper-evident evidence bundles and decision dossiers, which is the form of artefact an audit most wants to find already in place.
title: XAI-Compliance-by-Design: A Modular Framework for GDPR- and AI Act-Aligned Decision Transparency in High-Risk AI Systems

reading.body:
A modular framework can produce tamper-evident decision records for high-risk AI, but the evidence comes from a synthetic test, not a deployed system.

The design separates two flows. One covers data, models, explanations, and monitoring. The other covers policy, human oversight, audit, and decisions. A mapping matrix ties technical items to GDPR, the AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001, so each explanation and monitoring signal has a named rule behind it. The proof of concept used a Random Forest classifier, SHAP, LIME, and drift indicators on a synthetic intrusion-detection scenario, and it produced verifiable artefacts plus decision files.

For AI specifically, the useful claim is about form rather than accuracy. Audits want evidence that already exists in a checkable shape, and tamper-evident bundles are that shape. The framework does not claim a new detection algorithm, so its value sits in compliance readiness and oversight rather than model performance.

What the data does not cover is scale or operation. There is no real deployment, no production traffic, and no measured cost of running the pipeline. The citation count is three, which says little this early. The result is a demonstration that the artefacts can be generated, not proof that they survive contact with a live high-risk system.

explain_beginner: The paper presents a way to make high-risk AI decisions easier to check. Instead of adding explanations only after a model is built, it combines explanation tools, compliance rules, and careful machine learning operations from the start. The system has two connected parts: one handles data, models, explanations, and monitoring, while the other handles policy, human oversight, audits, and decisions. A test using a made-up intrusion detection example produced records that can show how a decision was made and whether the records were changed. This matters because organisations using AI in sensitive areas need evidence for regulators, auditors, and accountability.
explain_business: For executives, this paper suggests that high-risk AI used in security and privacy settings can be governed with evidence, not just model performance. The proposed framework ties technical explanations, monitoring data, and compliance records to specific rules in GDPR, the AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001. Its test showed that even a small example can produce verifiable records for audits and accountability. In practice, this supports decisions about whether to invest in a governance pipeline built around evidence, how to prepare for audits, and how to reduce reliance on one-off explanations. It does not claim a new detection algorithm, so the value is in compliance readiness and oversight.
explain_practitioner: The authors propose a modular architecture for high-risk AI, called XAI-Compliance-by-Design. It combines explainable AI methods, compliance-by-design ideas, and trustworthy MLOps. Two connected flows are used: one technical flow covers data, models, explanations, and monitoring, while a governance flow covers policy, human oversight, audit, and decisions. An engine for compliance by design and a matrix mapping technical items to regulations connect these flows to GDPR, the AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001. The Python proof of concept uses a synthetic intrusion-detection-inspired anomaly scenario, a Random Forest classifier, SHAP, LIME, drift indicators, and records designed to reveal tampering, plus decision files. It systematically produced verifiable artefacts supporting auditability and accountability.
